title: Word Problem Workshop
context: Grade 4, and the method is finished by now, so these two pages are about getting from a sentence to a sum. An adult sees word problems. What the page is actually doing is naming two separate decisions: what is being asked, and which of the printed numbers answer it. The page says outright that a problem may print a number that is not needed, which is a thing most books leave for a child to discover by being marked wrong.

writeup.why: Turn a problem written in sentences into a column sum, using only the numbers that answer what was asked.
writeup.look: A short problem at the top with every number liftable, and an empty column mat waiting underneath it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Word Problem Workshop' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many numbers are down on the mat against how many the question needs, two numbers side by side in ink, with the words of the chosen question card printed small underneath them once a card has been picked; on the third phase it carries the numbers that have been turned down as well, and on the fourth it marks which of the addends on the mat was built rather than lifted. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The problem board is 1086 by 156 at 64,202, the sentences set large on the paper colour with every number in them drawn as a card 130 by 56 standing proud of its line; a card lifted out leaves a ruled dash in the gap so the sentence still reads, and a card pushed back settles into the dash and fills it. On the second phase the board carries a table in the same rectangle instead, a heading row and three ruled rows 40 tall, and a whole row lifts off it as one piece. The question row is three cards 330 by 64 at 64,368, at 442,368 and at 820,368, each holding one plain wording of what might be being asked, and until one of them is picked no number card will lift at all. The column mat is 620 by 230 at 64,444: a heading row 34 tall of six ruled cells reading L, TTh, Th, H, T and O, a carry strip 32 tall above it where a carried digit stands small and vermilion over the column it is being added into, addend rows 48 tall that grow downward as cards land, a rule 4 tall under the last addend, and the sum row under the rule with its digits in green. A card lands on the mat by its right hand end, so a four digit addend under a five digit one leaves its left hand column standing empty rather than closing the gap up. The build bay is 380 by 230 at 716,444 and stays shut and outlined until the fourth phase, when it opens with two rows of its own, the printed amount above and the amount it is more by below, and drops the built card out of its foot with a drawn edge, so an addend that was made is told from an addend that was lifted for the rest of the sum. A number turned down dims in its sentence to the grey this chapter keeps for something holding a place and bringing nothing, which is exactly what that number is doing, and it keeps its outline so it can still be read and pointed at. The answer sentence strip is 1086 by 48 at 64,682, blank until the sum row is full, and it then writes the finished sum back into a sentence that answers the question card word for word. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever the sum has to be written, with a strip of unit words under them, tickets, people, books, crates and litres among them, because the answer sentence has to name what was counted. On the third phase one further key greys a number in its sentence, and on the fourth the build bay borrows the number keys while the described amount is worked out and hands them back when its card drops. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number being added is deep blue, the sum under the rule is green, a carried digit is vermilion and always drawn small above the column it is being added into, a rounded number and any estimated sum are rose, the digit under discussion or the one that is missing is amber, and a zero holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading over it before it is told by its band, and a carry is told by being small and sitting above the rule.
writeup.finish: The card shows the problem the child worked with its numbers sorted, the spare one still greyed, and the answer written as a sentence.

phases.win: the mat holds two addends and the answer is written back into a sentence
phases.does: picks the question card, lifts both numbers down and adds the columns
phases.goal: the amounts being put together come down onto the mat as addends
phases.says: Say what you are being asked for before you touch a number.
phases.check: Read me the problem, then tell me what it wants without saying any of its numbers.
phases.feels: a paragraph turns into two numbers, one under the other, and the sentences stop mattering
phases.hands: Read the problem aloud, turn the page face down, and ask the child to say what is being asked for in their own words before the page is turned back over.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what does your question card say? Second rung, the phase's: which two amounts does it put together? Third rung: the problem is cut to its question sentence alone with both number cards showing, and the child says which of them comes down. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: the numbers are the part a sum needs, so the sentences look like the part that can be skipped.
wrong.move: takes the numbers down in the order the sentences print them without ever saying what the question asks.
wrong.screen: the question cards lift together and the last sentence of the problem lights on the board, while every number card goes back up into the sentence it came from; no card will lift again until a question card has been picked. Nothing is marked and nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: the two numbers begin together on the line in the sentences, and beginning together is what lining up looks like.
wrong.move: lines a four digit addend up with a five digit one by their left ends, so every column is out by a place.
wrong.screen: the heading over every digit of the shorter card is named as it slides, and the card carries on sliding right until its last digit stands in the ones column, leaving its left hand column standing empty. The rule and the sum row stay empty while it moves, so nothing is added until the places agree.

phases.screen: a two sentence problem with two numbers in it and an empty mat
phases.soWhat: Say what is being asked, find the amounts being put together, line them up by their right ends and add the columns from the ones.
phases.concept: A word problem hides a column sum

phases.win: all three rows sit on the mat and none of them is left behind
phases.does: taps each row down in turn and adds the three addends
phases.goal: each row of a table is one addend
phases.says: Read the table across. Each row is one addend.
phases.check: How many addends is a table of three years, and how would you know if you had missed one?
phases.feels: a table turns into a column of addends, and the rows are suddenly the thing worth counting
phases.hands: Copy the table onto paper with a ruler, then rewrite it as a column of numbers with the places lined up, and count the rows of the table against the addends in the column.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many rows does the table have? Second rung, the phase's: how many cards are standing on your mat? Third rung: the table is cut to two rows and both are brought down before the third is put back. The pad stays open and nothing already on the mat is taken away.

wrong.why: a table read downwards ends wherever the eye stops, and two addends is what most of the sums so far have had.
wrong.move: brings the first two rows down, works the sum and stops, leaving the third row up in the table.
wrong.screen: the running count reads the rows that are down against the rows in the table and the two numbers do not agree; the rows that have come down are ruled through on the board while the row still up there keeps its full ink, so the one that was left behind is the only dark row on the table.

wrong.why: everything inside a table looks like part of the table, and a year is written in digits exactly as a count is.
wrong.move: brings a heading down onto the mat as though it were an amount to add.
wrong.screen: the row lifts whole and parts in the air above the mat: the heading half turns and settles on the mat's left margin as a label, and the amount half comes down into the columns by its right hand end, so each row gives one label and one addend and there is nowhere for a second number from that row to go.

phases.screen: a table of three rows with the mat empty beneath it
phases.soWhat: Each row of a table gives one addend, and every row has to come down before the sum is worked.
phases.concept: A table is a list of addends

phases.win: the spare number dims in its sentence and the mat holds only two addends
phases.does: greys the spare number and takes down only the two that are needed
phases.goal: a number can be printed and still have no job in the question
phases.says: One of these numbers has no job here. Which one?
phases.check: Point at the number in this problem you did not use, and tell me what it was there for.
phases.feels: a number can be perfectly true and still have no work to do in this sum
phases.hands: Read a problem with a pencil in hand, underline every number that answers the question, draw a light box round any number that does not, and say out loud what the boxed number is there for.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does your question card ask for? Second rung, the phase's: does this number help to answer it? Third rung: the problem is read back one sentence at a time with only that sentence's number liftable, so each is judged on its own. Nothing greyed is ever deleted.

wrong.why: the number is printed in the problem, and until now everything printed in a problem has been needed.
wrong.move: adds the hall's seating capacity in along with the two counts of people who came.
wrong.screen: the question card stays lit and each number card is held up against it in turn with the sentence it came from printed underneath; the capacity card is the only one whose sentence says what the hall could hold rather than who came in, and it settles back into its place in grey. The child's total stays in the slot beside the new one.

wrong.why: a number with no job looks like a mistake, and a mistake is a thing to rub out.
wrong.move: deletes the spare number off the board so the problem looks tidy.
wrong.screen: the number comes back into its sentence in grey with its outline still drawn round it, and the whole problem is read through once with it standing there; grey is the colour this chapter keeps for something holding a place and bringing nothing to the sum, which is precisely the job that number is doing.

phases.screen: a three number problem where one number answers nothing
phases.soWhat: Work out what is being asked first, take down only the numbers that answer it, and leave the spare one where it is.
phases.concept: Not every number printed is needed

phases.win: a new card appears on the mat carrying the amount that was never printed
phases.does: opens the build bay, works the described amount out and brings it down
phases.goal: a described amount is worked out before it can be added
phases.says: That day is described, not printed. Build it first.
phases.check: The second day had a thousand more visitors than the first. What is the first sum you would do, and what is the second?
phases.feels: a number the problem needs is nowhere on the page, and you make it yourself before you can use it
phases.hands: Read the sentence that describes the second amount and write it out as its own small sum on a separate line, finished and underlined, before the main sum is started at all.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which day is printed and which day is only described? Second rung, the phase's: what would you add to the printed one to get the other? Third rung: the build bay opens with the printed amount already in its upper row, so only the amount it is more by has to be found. The mat keeps whatever is already on it.

wrong.why: the two increases are the last numbers the problem mentions, so the sum that uses them feels like the last sum there is to do.
wrong.move: adds the thousand more and the hundred more onto the first day's total and hands that in as the answer for both days.
wrong.screen: the build bay shows what came out of it standing on a card of its own, and that card goes up onto the mat beside the first day's card so that two day cards are lying there, each with its own total printed on it; the mat plainly has two rows to add, and the child's number is printed beside the second of them. Nothing is marked.

wrong.why: every number used so far has been printed on the board, so a number that is needed ought to be somewhere there to find.
wrong.move: hunts the board for the second day's figure, waiting for it to be printed somewhere among the sentences.
wrong.screen: every number card on the board lifts a little and sets down again, and the sentence that describes the amount underlines itself word by word; the build bay then opens with its two empty rows and the words more than standing between them, so the place where the missing number has to be made is drawn rather than said.

phases.screen: a problem where one day is described as so many more than another
phases.soWhat: An amount described as so many more than another has to be built first, and only then can it go into the sum that was asked for.
phases.concept: Sometimes an addend has to be built first

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the described amount is built. The sentence that describes it lights word by word as the build bay fills, the printed day going into the upper row and the amount it is more by into the lower, and the small sum works itself there in its own columns. Then the card drops out of the foot of the bay with a drawn edge, rises back up to the board and settles into the sentence where the description was standing, so the problem can be read straight through with every number now printed in it. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a two sentence problem is printed across the board with its two numbers standing proud of the lines as cards, the row of question cards is face up beneath it, and the column mat below is ruled under its headings and empty. On the second the board carries a table of three rows in place of the sentences, ruled and complete, with the mat empty under it. On the third the problem runs to three numbers and all three stand proud, one of which answers nothing. On the fourth the build bay is drawn beside the mat with its two rows empty and the words more than standing between them, and one of the amounts in the problem is described in a sentence rather than printed as a card. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the row of question cards gives one slow lift while the voice asks what the question is actually asking for. That lift is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: A bank of problems in sentences, in tables and with described amounts, with a bay for writing your own. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on turning sentences and tables into sums, leaving the spare number out and building an addend.

observations.why: The question says which amounts are being put together, and only those amounts are addends.
observations.soWhat: Choosing the numbers is a step of its own, and it comes before any adding.
observations.observe: Picking the question card sorted the numbers before a single one had been lifted.

observations.why: A table is a list with one addend to a row, and a column sum does not know where its addends came from.
observations.soWhat: Every way of writing a problem ends at the same column mat.
observations.observe: A table came down as three addends and the mat looked exactly like the mat the sentences made.

observations.why: A number is printed because it is true, not because the question needs it.
observations.soWhat: I can turn a number down and still say afterwards why I turned it down.
observations.observe: The spare number stayed on the board in grey and the answer was right without it.

observations.why: That day was described as so many more than the day before, so it had to be built before it could be used.
observations.soWhat: Some of the numbers a problem needs are made rather than found.
observations.observe: One of the addends on the mat was never printed anywhere in the problem.

serves.exercise: finding the total number of students who appeared for the entrance examination
finding the total number of students in the two groups of grades

source_tool.description: A short problem sits at the top of the stage in ordinary sentences, with every number in it drawn as a card that can be lifted out. Below it is an empty column mat. The child reads the question, states what is being asked by picking from a short row of question cards, and only then starts lifting numbers down onto the mat. A number lifted down can be pushed back up again, so nothing is committed, and a spare number left in the sentence is greyed rather than removed, which keeps it visible as a thing that was considered and rejected. Some problems arrive as a table instead of sentences, and a table row taps down to the mat whole. Some describe an amount rather than printing it, and for those a build bay opens where the described amount is worked out first and comes down to the mat as a new card. When the mat is loaded the sum is worked in columns as usual and the answer is written back into a sentence, so the number that comes out is read as an answer to the question rather than as a total.
source_tool.art_direction: A short problem above an empty mat / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that tie themselves together, a rule under the last addend, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A sum is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the addends stacked with their right ends aligned, and a horizontal rule between the last addend and the sum. A bare row of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach adding.
A carried digit is always drawn small, above the column it is being added into, never in the margin and never below the rule.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number being added is deep blue, the sum under the rule is green, and a digit carried into the next column is vermilion, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A rounded number and any estimated sum are rose, so an estimate is told apart from an exact answer before either is read. The digit under discussion, which is usually the one that is missing, is amber. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a carry is told apart by being small and sitting above its column before it is told apart by its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the problem again, one sentence at a time, with your question card showing.
voice.onNext: A new problem. Say what is being asked before you touch a number.
voice.opening: Read it through first. What is the question actually asking for?
voice.onFinish: Every problem turned into a sum, and the numbers you turned down are still there to see.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Sentences, tables, described amounts, and a bay for writing your own.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A word problem hides a column sum
A table is a list of addends
Not every number printed is needed
Sometimes an addend has to be built first

placement.where: After two word problems have been done on paper and at least one has gone wrong for the right reason. The tool is what makes the choosing of the numbers a visible step rather than something that happens silently in a child's head.

answer_key.rule: Say what is being asked before touching a number. Then take down only the numbers that answer it, leaving any spare number where it is. A table is a list of addends, one to a row. An amount that is described rather than printed, such as so many more than the day before, has to be worked out first and then used. Line the chosen addends up by their right ends and add the columns from the ones, and write the answer back into a sentence.
answer_key.wrong: The problem is read again one sentence at a time with the question card left showing, and the numbers go back up into the sentences so the choosing can be done again. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The question asks for the two days put together, so both numbers are addends.
Line them up by their right ends: 9,365 is shorter, so its left column stays empty.
Adding the columns from the ones gives 21,845.
items.question: A fair sold 12,480 tickets on Saturday and 9,365 tickets on Sunday. How many tickets were sold over the two days?
items.checkpoint: The amounts being put together are the addends, however the sentences are worded.
items.misconception: Lining 12,480 and 9,365 up by their left ends, because one has five digits and the other four.

steps: Each year is one row of the table, so there are three addends.
Take all three down onto the mat with their right ends lined up.
Adding the columns gives 74,823, with a carry out of the ones, the tens and the thousands.
items.question: A nursery raised 18,240 saplings in the first year, 26,175 in the second and 30,408 in the third. What is the total?
items.checkpoint: A table gives one addend per row, and every row has to come down.
items.misconception: Adding the first two years and stopping, because a table read downwards can lose its last line.

steps: The question asks how many people came in, not how many could have.
So the two numbers that answer it are 1,640 and 2,185.
Adding those two gives 3,825, and the 5,000 seats stay greyed in the sentence.
items.answer: 3,825 people, and the seating capacity is not needed
items.question: A hall seats 5,000 people. One evening 1,640 adults and 2,185 children came in. How many people came in?
items.checkpoint: Work out what is being asked first, then choose only the numbers that answer it.
items.misconception: Adding the 5,000 seats in as well, because the number is printed in the problem.

steps: The second day is not printed and has to be built: 10,340 men and 1,720 women, which is 12,060.
items.question: At a health camp, 9,340 men and 1,620 women came on the first day. On the second day a thousand more men and a hundred more women came than on the first. How many people came over the two days?
items.checkpoint: An amount that is described has to be built before it can be added.
items.misconception: Answering 12,060, which is the second day alone, because the two increases were added and the first day was never brought back in.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.

items.question: A depot loaded 7,205 crates in the morning and 6,318 crates in the afternoon. How many crates in all?
A village has 4,806 men and 5,127 women. What is its population?

items.final_answer: 6,214 passengers. The 60 seats are not needed

items.question: A child solved a problem by using all three of its printed numbers and got a total far larger than the answer. What should the child have done first?
items.final_answer: Worked out what the question was asking, and then taken down only the numbers that answer it, leaving the spare one where it was

items.question: A stadium counted 21,345 spectators on Friday. On Saturday a thousand more came than on Friday. How many came over the two days?
A library lent 12,608 books in January, a hundred more than that in February, and a thousand more than February in March. How many books were lent over the three months?
items.final_answer: 39,024 books, because February was 12,708 and March was 13,708

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: states what the problem is asking before any number moves
takes a number out of the sentence and down onto the mat
returns a number to its sentence, so nothing is committed
dims a number that is not needed while leaving it readable
taps a whole row of a table down to the mat as one addend
works out an amount that is described rather than printed
writes the finished sum back into a sentence that answers the question

teaching_notes: Make the question card a real step and do not let anybody skip it. A child who has said out loud what is being asked has already sorted the numbers; a child who has not will add whatever is printed. Keep the spare number greyed rather than deleted, because the point is not that the number vanishes but that it was looked at and turned down. When a table comes up, read it across with a finger and count the rows before any of them come down, since a table read downwards is how the last line gets lost. The build bay is the hardest phase and the one most worth the time: an amount described as so many more than another is not on the page, and a child who adds the extra amount to the total at the end has answered a different question. Finish every problem with the answer sentence read aloud. A number with no sentence round it is not yet an answer.
generation_prompt: Build a word problem tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A short problem in sentences sits across the top with every number in it drawn as a liftable card, and an empty ruled column mat waits below. A row of question cards states what the problem is asking and must be chosen before any number can be lifted. Numbers drag down to the mat and push back up again, and a grey the spare control dims a number in place, keeping it readable rather than removing it. Some problems arrive as a small table instead, where a whole row taps down to the mat as one addend. A build bay opens for problems that describe an amount instead of printing it, works that amount out in its own small sum, and sends the result down as a new card. The loaded mat adds its columns from the ones with carries drawn in circles, and an answer sentence control writes the finished sum back into a sentence that answers the question card. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Read the problem and pick the card that says what it is asking. Lift only the numbers that answer it down onto the mat, and grey out any number that has no job. If a number is described rather than printed, build it first. Add the columns, then write your answer back into a sentence.
